item.title: Leadership Recovery Requires More Than Leaving the Office
item.description:
Leadership

Leadership Recovery Requires More Than Leaving the Office

Why sustainable leaders need protected spaces where the role cannot follow them.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Leadership recovery requires more than physically leaving the office.
  • Leaders can be away from work and still remain mentally inside the role.
  • Protected spaces help leaders recover attention, judgment, and emotional capacity.
  • Sustainable leaders design boundaries so the role has somewhere else to go.
Sustainable leaders need protected spaces where the role cannot follow them.
Source: Jeff Frey / Used with permission

In one of my research interviews with a leader, he described running as one of the few parts of the day that truly belonged to him.

“First of all, it’s my time,” he said. “It’s the hour, hour and a half in the day that’s mine.”

One day, rain pushed him into his organization’s fitness center instead of outside at home before work. He was on the treadmill early in the morning when someone next to him began asking work questions. He understood why. He was the leader. He was visible. He was right there.

But it was 5 a.m.

He was not at his desk, not in a meeting, and technically in his "off" hours. He wasn’t “in the office,” exactly. But because he was working out inside the building, he said, “I’m on.”

The problem was not that anyone did anything wrong. It was that the role had followed him into one of the few spaces he counted on for recovery.

Sustainable leaders do not just need time away from work. They need protected spaces where the role cannot follow them.

Recovery Is More Than Absence

Many leaders assume that if they are not officially working, they are recovering.

But recovery is not only about being absent from the office. It is about what happens inside the mind and body when work no longer has immediate access to your attention.

Research on recovery from work identifies psychological detachment as one of the key recovery experiences, along with relaxation, mastery, and control (Sonnentag & Fritz, 2007). People do not fully recover simply because they stop performing tasks. They recover when they can mentally disconnect long enough for energy, attention, and judgment to return.

Though a leader can leave the building, close the laptop, say goodbye to coworkers, or walk into the gym, that same leader can still be mentally replaying the scenarios of the day. Work still sits just beneath a thin surface of recovery. One question, text, decision, or interruption can pull the leader right back up into the role.

Just like a plant that receives only a little water at a time develops shallow roots, a leader with only surface-level recovery can be uprooted quickly. But leaders, like plants, need a deeper soak to develop deeper roots.

The Role Can Follow You

For many leaders, the role is now highly portable. Text, email, messaging platforms, and flexible work tools are great because they allow leaders to respond from anywhere and stay connected when needed.

article continues after advertisement

These connections, however, also create what researchers call the autonomy paradox. Mazmanian, Orlikowski, and Yates found that mobile devices appear to give professionals more control over when and where they work, but in actuality, these devices increase the expectations of constant connection (Mazmanian, Orlikowski, & Yates, 2013). That sounds like less control.

Another leader in my research described the difference it made when he separated his personal phone from his work phone. The work phone could stay on the desk. He could turn it off. On vacation, no one could reach him for two weeks. “If something truly serious happens,” he said, “I would hear about it on the news.”

He came back with energy, ideas, and a stronger desire to lead.

Protected Spaces Are Built

Most leaders already know they need space from work. The harder question is whether they believe they are allowed to protect it.

Work-nonwork boundary management research points to the importance of perceived boundary control (Kossek, Ruderman, Braddy, & Hannum, 2012). A leader may truly want more separation but still feel unable to enforce it because of organizational expectations, staffing gaps, client needs, board pressure, or the leader’s own internal sense of responsibility. They let the role follow them.

That is why telling a leader to “set better boundaries” doesn’t always work.

If that story about a leader being unreachable for a couple of weeks bothered you, you may be one of these “responsible” leaders. Here’s where to start to improve your work recovery time. Ask yourself:

  1. Where does the role keep following me when I am trying to recover?
  2. What situations reach me only because we have never made a different plan?
  3. Who needs to be trained and trusted so the role has somewhere else to go besides me?
article continues after advertisement

Those questions turn recovery from a wish into a leadership design problem that you and your staff can solve.

Kreiner, Hollensbe, and Sheep studied how people negotiate the work-home interface through boundary work tactics, including physical, temporal, behavioral, and communicative practices (Kreiner, Hollensbe, & Sheep, 2009). What does this look like in real life? I personally have a physical boundary that I do not stay in the event hotel of a conference or corporate event where I am a keynote or a prominent figure. Why? Because the hallways, elevators, and yes, the gym, inevitably become spaces where I am accessible even when I am no longer on stage.

A temporal boundary might mean protecting dinner time. A behavioral boundary might mean making a habit out of leaving the office at the same time each day. A communicative boundary might mean changing “I’m away but checking email” to “I’m away. For this issue, contact this person. For that issue, contact that person.”

That is not neglect. That is intentional leadership structure.

Protected spaces are not places where nothing important exists. They are places where the role has been given somewhere else to go until you choose to let it back in.

Protect the Spaces That Restore You

Sustainable leadership does not mean relinquishing responsibility.

Sustainable leadership means recognizing that leaders need intentional, frequent, and repeated deep recovery spaces. That could be running, meals, phone-free blocks of time, or an auto-reply that routes responsibility instead of pretending to be away while remaining available.

Those real, protected spaces help leaders recover attention, renew judgment, reconnect with people outside the office, and return with more capacity for the work that matters.

Protecting those spaces does not mean you care less about the mission. You are protecting them because you care enough to put yourself in the best position possible to lead.

To lead sustainably, protect the spaces where the role cannot follow you, so you can recover, refocus, and return ready to lead.

item.title: When Did Your Relationship Become So Serious?
item.description:
Relationships

When Did Your Relationship Become So Serious?

Why long-term couples need more spontaneity, silliness, and shared laughter.

Posted August 10, 2026

Key points
  • Long-term partners can become capable co-managers while losing touch with playfulness.
  • Shared humor helps couples connect outside their usual roles and responsibilities.
  • Small, spontaneous moments can restore lightness without becoming another task.
  • Play cannot repair serious hurt, but it can balance stress with connection and joy.

When was the last time you and your partner did something that served absolutely no purpose beyond making you laugh? Did you have to think about it for a while? If so, you’re in pretty good company these days.

In 2026, people are increasingly tired of hyper-curated profiles, strategized conversations, and first dates that could easily double as job interviews – which is exactly why “whimsy” is one of this year’s bigger dating trends so far. The general idea is pretty simple. Just leave a little room for spontaneity and silliness, as well as for random detours that translate into really great stories to tell later.

This isn’t just great advice for singles still getting to know each other, either. If anything, long-term couples can benefit from it even more.

When Partners Become Co-Managers

Responsibilities have a way of accumulating in long-term relationships. There are always bills to pay, appointments to remember, broken objects to repair, or relatives to worry about, and there always will be.

Eventually, those same two people who could once stay up until 2 a.m. talking about nearly anything realize most of their conversations now revolve around essentials that need to be handled by next Thursday. Transitions like these are also normal and even desirable to some extent. Managing a fruitful shared life is part of intimacy, so healthy relationships need two people involved who cooperate and plan.

The problems start when “management mode” becomes the default. Loving partners can become excellent co-administrators of a household while also losing touch with the unique companionship that launched their entire relationship. They might communicate well, but also completely stop playing and spending time together outside of a planned agenda.

Why Play Is Important in Adult Relationships

Playfulness might not sound that important compared to the serious business of maintaining a relationship, but laughter and play actually serve essential functions.

Play presents opportunities for partners to experience each other outside the confines of their usual roles. For just a little while, no one has to be the responsible parent, the person who worries about the bank balance, or the one who always remembers to call the plumber. Instead, they can simply enjoy one another’s company.

Shared humor also helps create small pockets of connection and happiness during stressful periods. Naturally, a well-timed inside joke or the occasional five-minute detour for whimsy’s sake isn’t going to eliminate the pressures couples face. It can support balance by giving them another type of emotional experience to share alongside those pressures.

article continues after advertisement

There should always be limits involved, of course, as playfulness doesn’t erase issues like contempt, betrayal, emotional disconnect, or unresolved hurt. Both partners need to be capable of navigating difficult conversations, apologizing, acknowledging pain, and seeking professional support when necessary.

However, a relationship that’s solely focused on identifying and solving problems is in danger of also becoming one in which the people involved have forgotten they’re allowed to enjoy each other.

Bringing Back Fun Without Scheduling Fun

Turning playfulness into another relationship improvement project to add to a to-do list is the quickest way to drain the life out of it. There’s nothing wrong with planned date nights and new shared hobbies, but small alternatives are enough to bring some of the light back to a relationship.

Follow pointless impulses

Adults are experts at dismissing ideas that don’t serve some larger practical purpose. Try deliberately pursuing one anyway. Go ahead and take the scenic route home or buy the weird snack at the grocery store. Stop somewhere you’ve always wondered about and experience it together.

Revive your private language

The longer a couple has been together, the more inside jokes, weird references no one else would get, and random stories they eventually accumulate. Use them. Go out of your way to send ridiculous memes or photos that remind you of private jokes. Play your favorite songs while eating dinner.

Every tiny callback is a reminder that your relationship contains a whole world that belongs only to you.

Let ordinary moments be playful

It’s easier than you think to fit fun into the small spaces already available in your life. Turn household chores into competitive games, or let a quick conversation wander off on a million tangents just for fun. Use your imagination. (No planning necessary!)

article continues after advertisement

And make sure you both also resist the urge to test whether any of this is working. Play loses something vital when it becomes just another metric for tracking relationship health. Sometimes the healthiest thing you can do together is waste a little time (and enjoy every minute of it).
